Key visual observations:
- Soybean trifoliate with brown/tan irregular lesions scattered across all three leaflets
- Some lesions appear angular in shape
- Yellow/chlorotic areas around some lesions (particularly on right lower leaflet)
- Spots of varying sizes, some coalescing
- Appears to be on younger/lower canopy foliage

Top candidates: **Bacterial_Blight** (angular spots with yellow-green halos), **Septoria_brown_spot** (angular red-brown spots with yellowing), **Frogeye_leaf_spot** (circular-angular spots with reddish borders), **Bacterial_Pustule**.

Now I have all 21 reference images viewed. Let me synthesize my analysis.

**Test image key features:**
- Soybean trifoliate, photographed from above (lower canopy small plant)
- Multiple irregular/angular tan-to-brown lesions scattered across all three leaflets
- Some lesions show yellowing (chlorotic halos) around them, particularly the lower-right leaflet
- Lesion size varies from small specks to medium-larger irregular patches
- No white powder, no purple discoloration, no shot-holes, no stem/root symptoms visible

**Candidate comparison:**
- **Septoria_brown_spot**: Angular red-to-brown spots, starts lower canopy progressing upward, surrounded by yellowing, tiny pycnidia. The reference lower-right panel showed a similar pattern on a young plant. Matches well.
- **Bacterial_Blight**: Angular water-soaked spots with yellow-green halos. Reference showed very small early-stage yellow-green spots (less brown/necrotic than test image). More common on upper young leaves.
- **Phyllosticta_leaf_spot**: Gray/tan irregular lesions with dark margins. Reference showed grayish necrotic lesions, but less consistent pattern than Septoria.
- **Frogeye_leaf_spot**: Circular spots with reddish-purple borders, shot-holes — not matching the angular irregular pattern.

**Conclusion**: The angular, red-to-brown spots with surrounding chlorosis on what appears to be lower canopy foliage matches **Septoria_brown_spot** most closely. The progression pattern (lower canopy, scattered spots with yellowing) aligns well with Septoria's characteristic early-season, bottom-up progression.
